summary: Spain's brick 'castle' light of 1892 at Puerto Rico's westernmost point was wrecked by the 1918 earthquake; a concrete tower, lit in 1922, still carries its lantern.

structures.note: Spanish octagonal brick tower within a one-story brick and stone dwelling; wrecked by the 1918 earthquake.
Cylindrical tower placed in commission 12 January 1922; carries the lantern of the first lighthouse.
Double dwelling of two four-room quarters, 63 by 26 ft; abandoned after automation and later destroyed by fire.

access.note: Grounds open daily as a municipal park; the tower is closed. The Coast Guard is custodian of the lighthouse.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (custodian); Municipality of Rincon (park, under lease)

events.note: Spain approves a plan for 14 lighthouses in Puerto Rico that names Punta Higuero; no money until 1875, and then for other sites.
Revised Spanish plan ranks Punta Higuero tenth in order of construction, after Punta de la Tuna.
Spanish brick tower and dwelling commenced 1891, finished 1892 at a cost of 12,361 pesos; designed by Jose Maria Sainz (Mari Mut).
Sixth-order Fresnel lens (USLHS; Light-House Board 1901). The NRHP nomination also describes a fourth-order Bernard & Barbier lens, 50 cm across.
Entered service 17 January 1893 (Mari Mut); 13 January 1893 (Lighthousefriends); the NRHP nomination gives only 1892. A newspaper of 21 September 1893 shows a keeper at the light.

Light-House Board directed on 1 May 1900 to take charge of the Porto Rican lights; fifteen lights counted on the island in the Board's report for fiscal 1900, with the service being assimilated to the general Light-House Service.
Listed among lights changed from fixed to flashing or occulting, illuminant changed from oil to incandescent oil vapor (Bulletin, August 1913).
Detached, fireproof oil house built (Lighthousefriends).
Ninth-district efficiency pennant for fiscal year 1914 awarded to Point Jiguero, keeper Jose Prieto (Bulletin, January 1915).
Earthquake and tidal wave, 10:20 a.m. on 11 October 1918; station 'practically wrecked'; dwelling abandoned; further shocks on 24 October, 11 and 12 November added cracks.
Local notice to mariners of 6 November 1918: light repaired and restored to its former characteristic (white, group flashing, three flashes every fifteen seconds).
Earthquake at 4:39 a.m. on 22 August 1919 (4.5 minutes) broke the mantle and put the light out temporarily.

Sundry civil act of 19 July 1919 appropriates $24,000 for rebuilding the station; bids invited in December 1919 and rejected as too high (Bulletin, March 1920); work done by district force, hired labor and purchased material.
Earthquakes on 26 January and 10 February 1920 broke mantles; on 10 February the light was out 42 minutes while the vaporizer was changed.
Frame dwelling for two keepers finished and reinforced-concrete tower built by district force and hired labor.
New reinforced-concrete tower placed in commission 12 January 1922 (Commissioner of Lighthouses; Bulletin says 9 January); old lantern reused.
Keeper Rufino Flores Graniel aided a workman with a knee wound at the railroad track near the station (20 November; reported in the Bulletin of 2 February 1925).
Keeper Graniel assisted four persons whose boat reached the station after four days adrift (9 August 1925).
Hurricane of 22-29 July 1926 crossed southwest Puerto Rico on the evening of 23 July; keeper Graniel sheltered 24 people.
Old Spanish building (by then a school, tower removed) demolished per Mari Mut; the NRHP nomination and OECH give 1922.
Light made automatic and left unattended; keepers' house and support buildings abandoned and later destroyed by fire.
Name changed from Faro de Punta Higuero to Faro de Punta Higuera, per Rincon's municipal page.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 October 1981 (NRIS 81000560).
HAER written data (HAER No. PR-21) prepared by Kevin Murphy from the 1979 nomination.
Municipality of Rincon leases the lighthouse from the Coast Guard to administer, maintain and restore it.
Restored and turned into a passive park with maritime museum, cafe, huts and lookout (Rincon municipal page).

corrections.why: The HAER written data at loc.gov/item/pr0044 are headed 'HAER No. PR-21'; 'pr0044' is the Library of Congress item id, not the HAER number.

The Light-House Board says the Spanish work was finished in 1892; Mari Mut (17 January) and Lighthousefriends (13 January) say the light entered service in January 1893; a newspaper of 21 September 1893 shows a keeper at the light.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Construction was commenced in 1891 and finished in 1892 (Light-House Board 1901); the light entered service in January 1893 (17th per Mari Mut, 13th per Lighthousefriends). The NRHP nomination and Wikidata give the construction year, 1892.

The NRHP nomination and OECH say it was demolished in 1922 when the new tower was built; Mari Mut says the tower was removed after the lantern moved in 1921, the building served as a school, and it was demolished in 1931 (footing removed in the mid-1990s).

resolved_conflicts.field: date new tower placed in commission
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Commissioner's report for fiscal 1922 and Mari Mut say 12 January 1922; the Bulletin's construction column says 9 January.

Light-House Board (1901) and USLHS: sixth-order fixed light. The NRHP nomination calls the station sixth order but describes a fourth-order Bernard & Barbier lens, 50 cm across; it also says the lens was destroyed in 1918, while the Commissioner (1922) says the lens apparatus removed from the old station was to go in the new lantern and Mari Mut says a 1922 report suggests the lens survived.

The Commissioner's report for fiscal 1920 (p. 49) reads 'appropriated $21,000' in the OCR; the Bulletin of March 1920, and the Commissioner's reports for 1921 and 1922, give $24,000 (act of 19 July 1919). $24,000 is used.

resolved_conflicts.field: date of the July 1926 hurricane over southwest Puerto Rico
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Bulletin of 1 September 1926 puts the storm over the southwest on the evening of 23 July; Lighthousefriends says the eye passed on 24 July.

resolved_conflicts.field: year Graniel aided the injured workman
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The item appears in the Bulletin of 2 February 1925 among events of November, so 20 November 1924; Lighthousefriends places it three months after the August 1925 rescue.

notes_for_editor: Core chronology (Spanish work 1891-92, 1918 earthquake, rebuilding 1919-22, automation 1933, 1981 NRHP, 1993 lease and park) rests on primary reports and agrees across sources. Open points: (1) the day the light first showed (13 or 17 January 1893) and whether any Spanish document gives it; (2) the lens order (sixth vs fourth) and whether the old lens survived; (3) when the old Spanish building was demolished (1922 vs 1931). The roster is the USLHS list (NARA registers via Kraig Anderson's inventory). Only Jose Prieto and Rufino Flores Graniel are confirmed in a primary record (Lighthouse Service Bulletin) at this station. Julio L. Rengel: the Bulletin of 1916 (PDF p. 50) names a 'Julio L. Rengel, keeper' of Culebrita Island Light Station in the hurricane of 9-10 October 1916; he is probably the Jiguero keeper of 1917-19 but no source says so, so it is not entered in other_stations. Spanish-era keepers are unnamed anywhere I looked (one unnamed torrero appears in a September 1893 newspaper). Spanish archives (Archivo General de Puerto Rico, Madrid ministry files), Mari Mut's sources (Castaldi 2013; Sanchez Terry 1992) and the Official Register were not consulted. The 1908 Chronicling America hit for 'Point Jiguero' (La Correspondencia, 7 Jan 1908, p. 2) was not read. The record's current characteristic (Oc W 4s, 27.4 m, 9 nm) was not verified against the Light List; Mari Mut (2009-2013) says the light is a small solar-powered lamp and USLHS lists a 250 mm current optic. Lighthousefriends' account of the 1918 inspection (cracks 2 and 8 ft above the dwelling roof, $30,000 request, concrete yoke) appears to come from a primary report I could not locate in the corpus. No new photos were added. The nomination, OECH sheet and HAER data pages all use 'Higuero'; local usage since 1953 is 'Higuera' (Rincon municipal page). Fact-check 2026-10-21: Rincon's municipal page (El Faro) says the lighthouse was 'destroyed again in 1931 and rebuilt again', a claim no other source supports (Mari Mut gives a 1931 demolition of the first building); the story reports it as the municipal page's version. The Rincon tourism page gives the Bonus plant as built 1960, operating 1962-1968; Lighthousefriends gives built 1960-1964, decommissioned 1970 (story gives both). Lighthousefriends names the Bonus plant nowhere; the name comes from the municipal pages. The USLHS roster span for Julio L. Rengel (at least 1917 to at least 1919) brackets 11 October 1918, but no primary record at this station names him.
